A major wrestling promotion is not at the late stage of its rival WCW, but we are firmly in the middle of 1999 WCW. 1998 was a high point for WCW and a good redemption following the screwed up ending to Starrcade 1997.

In 1998, they moved away from Hogan, put the title on Goldberg, and let him dominate all the way to Starrcade. Goldberg defending against Nash was a huge main event, and well worthy of their biggest show of the year. Nash was over. Goldberg was over. The NWO's influence had started to wane. They were right where they needed to be. The ending of Starrcade 1998 wasn't the greatest choice, but Goldberg had to lose the streak eventually and having Hall screw him out of it with the Cattle Prod was a way to set the stage for an explosive 1999 with Nash as champion and Goldberg chasing for his second reign.

Then something went horribly wrong. They started 1999 with the Fingerpoke of Doom, had Nash basically GIVE the title to Hulk Hogan, and reunite the NWO. Instead of giving Goldberg a title shot, he got bumped over to a feud with Hall since Hall was the one who hit him with the Cattle Prod. Hogan decided that his new title was SO important that he didn't even defend it at the first PPV in 1999. Hogan started feuding with Flair. Goldberg floundered and wandered off to aimlessly feud with other people instead of getting his title shot.. Things were never really the same again after that.

That's where we are right now in WWE, except they have no hot star to move the title to. Kofi was great for the title chase, but it was a novelty reign at best and now he's feuding with Dolph Ziggler. Seth didn't get a proper build towards Wrestlemania because the company was too focused on the Women's Main Event, and now they're making him look like a chump every time Brock shows up with the briefcase. Brock... He's over with the crowd, but Brock doesn't have enough dates on his contract to be a legitimate champion. Seth's feuding w/ Corbin who has worse go-away heat that Jinder Mahal and that's saying a lot while simultaneously feuding w/ a Brock.

Guys get good runs in NXT, then fade into obscurity on the Main Roster. Who is going to be left in 10 years to carry the company? Everyone who gets a little traction in the indies gets picked up and they aren't pushing them, so...where will we be in 10 years when they've ruined all the "next big things" and it's time for this generation to retire? That's going to be a noticeable problem before long.

Wrestling has always been a business that was built around the performers making the most money possible in the shortest amount of time while working the least number of dates.

It's why a top star signed with a rival promotion, it's why a popular tag team jumped ship.  It's why loads of guys in a major promotion wanted out of their contract so they could go to a competitor and get a piece of the pie.  Even guys who are loyalists would prefer competition.  It doesn't matter if you've been in the major promotion for 10 months or 10 years.  Nobody grows up with dreams of being a professional wrestling jobber for the rest of their life making pennies in exchange for possibly not being able to walk when their 55.  They want the fame, glory, but most importantly...the really big bank account.  They may ENJOY performing for the fans but it doesn't change the fact that they want the financial security that goes along with it, especially when they get older and have a family to support.  Even a guy like a highly skilled performer who was making loads of money on the indies and resisted the major promotion for a very long time was swayed by the temptation of finishing his career out with the owner and making lots of money in the process.  The money was so good that he signed on for one more year.

If your a professional wrestler, the smartest thing you can do right now is express interest in a new competitor.  Even if you want to stay in the major promotion, you literally *have* to sit down with the new promotion's owner and hear his offer. You *have* to use them as a bargaining chip to get more money from the major promotion.  Thing is, somewhere in that mix, is going to be a guy that the new competitor considers to be more valuable than the major promotion.  It might be someone like a well-known underutilized star, a former champion, a technical wizard, etc.  Someone that has huge potential and a big fan following, but the major promotion has left them in the midcard instead of pushing them.  Those are the guys the new competitor should target and the guys who are more likely to get a better offer from the new competitor than the major promotion.  Unfortunately, the new competitor can only take so many, and if the major promotion has already ruined their name value by jobbing them out for 5-7 years, then the new competitor can't bring them in and push them.  That's where a previous competitor went wrong.

I think the perspective is a bit skewed.  This may be an unpopular opinion, but John Cena was *not* a draw.  Keep your finger off the downvote for a second a hear me out.

John Cena's rise to prominence began between Wrestlemania 20 and Wrestlemania 21.  After defeating Big Show at 20, he had US Title feuds for much of the year, which included the introduction of the "Spinner" US Championship belt.  At 21, he won the WWE Championship and converted it to the "Spinner" WWE Championship.  WM 21 was Cena's first big championship win, but he didn't main event the show.  That honor went to Batista vs HHH.

Between 21 and 22, they had a major shift in the dynamic.  Cena was becoming the *top star* so they moved him to RAW, and started building him on the A-Show.  At WM 23, he defended against HHH and made The Game tap out.  This was a major accomplishment and the first 100% clear indicator that John Cena was the future of the company.  He was on the A-Show and he tapped HHH.  At WM 24, they further solidified it by having him tap Shawn Michaels.  Anyone who had followed wrestling understood that HHH & HBK didn't tap to anyone, so having John Cena tap them both at back-to-back WMs was a very clear sign that the company was firmly built around him for years to come.

Here's where it gets interesting.  Let's look at the ratings and flip back to 2005 when Cena's ascension began.  Raw hit a 4.0+ rating 17 times in 2005.  In 2006, after Cena tapped HHH?  Raw hit a 4.0+ rating 27 times.  If you look at that, then the ratings say Cena did VERY well, except he didn't.  There was a lot of interest early in the year, but by the end of the year?  WWE drew their last 4.0+ rating on August 21, 2006.  They literally went 4+ months w/o drawing a 4.0 rating at the end of the year, which included one of the lowest rated Raw EVER up to that point at a 2.7.  You can argue that it was Christmas Day, and that's a valid argument, but the December 26th show the previous year drew 3.7.  Blame the 1.0 drop on Christmas Day?  I would.  It just makes sense...sorta.

2007 is the year where Cena is FIRMLY in the top spot.  He's already tapped HHH and at WM, he tapped HBK.  They only had 11 4.0+ rated episodes of Raw in 2007.  The dropped below 3.0 on a random day in October.  Their Christmas Eve show was 2.5, which was lower than Christmas Day the previous year.

Okay, so now we're in 2008.  Cena's still at the top of the card.  How many times did they score a 4.0+ rating in 2008?  ZERO.  Not a single damn episode of Raw.  In fact, they went below 3.0 several times.  Cena hurt the company TREMENDOUSLY in 2008.

The company rebounded a little bit in 2009.  They had 4 episodes of Raw where they scored a 4.0+ rating, but that's a far cry from where they were a few years prior before they started force-feeding John Cena to the audience as the face of the company.

So, that's my take.  I don't think Cena helped the company.  I think the company forced him down everyone's throat and retained the portion of their audience that was willing to stay, while losing a lot of it.

He also mentions things like wheelchairs, loss of bladder control, etc., all the things that go along with severe spinal stenosis, which could occur from one bad bump and a dislocated vertebra or ligament damage. Spinal stenosis basically translates into a narrowing of the spinal canal. It can't be cured, but the symptoms can be alleviated. It's also something that everyone tends to get as they age, just from general wear/tear/daily activity.

If you want to understand the reason behind the retirement(s), you have to look at it like this:

Imagine you're 35 and the doctor tells you that due to the injuries you've sustained, your neck looks like someone who is in their late 50s and based on the general progression, it'll look like someone who is in their 70s by the time you're 45 if you keep taking bumps. He also mentions things like wheelchairs, loss of bladder control, etc., all the things that go along with severe spinal stenosis, which could occur from one bad bump and a dislocated vertebra or ligament damage. That kind of shit freaks you the fuck out and you realize you got money, so it isn't really worth the risk. Boom, you're retired.

Now, 9-10 years goes by. You're 45, which is the age the doctor said you would have the neck of a 70 year old if you kept going, and you've stopped wrestling entirely during that time. The doctor reevaluates you and has GOOD news. You still have the neck of someone in their 50s, but it's improved...more like early 50s instead of late 50s. You've had tremendous progress with stem cell treatments and the long break has lessened the damage that was caused when you used to be in the ring.

Having neck of someone in their early 50s at 45 isn't nearly as bad as having that neck when you're 35. The industry has also shifted drastically since you used to wrestle. People are making tons of money. There are Saudi paydays. Vince has caved on his whole 'full time or nothing' schedule that he used to offer everyone back then. There's something called a 'Brock schedule' now and an 'Orton contract' which allows limited work for maximum pay.

Is it a risk? Sure. Getting in the ring is always a risk, but there's a thing called risk vs reward, and if you can get a really nice reward for working less dates in a year than you used to work in a month, then sometimes it's worth it...especially if you can go out on YOUR terms versus being forced to retire due to an injury.

Also, it's worth pointing out that when Edge retired, a lot of wrestlers said they were working with necks that were in a lot worse shape, but didn't have the financial ability to just retire like Edge did.
